# Vegetable fermentation

This field note explains lactic acid fermentation. Its central process is salt encourages desirable bacteria while suppressing spoilage. Practitioners pay attention to the surrounding conditions before interpreting a single observation. A useful working method involves submerge shredded cabbage under brine in a clean vessel. This is not simply a matter of collecting a number: observations need enough context to distinguish a persistent pattern from a temporary change.

An important interpretation is that lactic acid lowers the pH and develops a sour flavor. For a practical assessment, document when and where the observation was made, the equipment or materials involved, and any unusual conditions. Compare measurements taken using the same method rather than assuming that unrelated measurements are directly comparable. Recording changes over time also helps explain whether an intervention is having its intended effect.

There is an important limitation: surface mold or an offensive odor warrants discarding the batch. When conditions change, revisit the original assumptions instead of applying the same response automatically. A careful operator checks equipment, records the relevant circumstances, and looks for independent evidence before drawing conclusions. Reports should distinguish what was observed from what is inferred and describe any uncertainty that could affect the decision.

The best procedure depends on the actual situation and the people responsible for it. Where a result has consequences for safety, conservation, or expensive equipment, use the appropriate local guidance and consult a qualified specialist. The examples in this note illustrate the principles rather than providing an exhaustive operating manual.
